notes.text: I will not — By asking a sign, as if I questioned the truth of his word: but this was deep hypocrisy.

David — He reproves them all, because they were the king's counsellors. Is it a small thing - Is it not wickedness enough. My God - To vex God's prophets and people, with your oppressions and horrid impieties. And by your ingratitude and unbelief, and disobedience of his commands.

Therefore — Because you despise me, and the sign which I now offer to you, God of his own free grace will send you a more honourable messenger, and give you a nobler sign. A sign - Of your deliverance. But how was this birth, which was not to happen 'till many ages after, a sign of their deliverance from present danger? This promised birth supposed the preservation of that city, and nation and tribe, in and of which the Messiah was to be born; and therefore there was no cause to fear that ruin which their enemies now threatened. Immanuel - God with us; God dwelling among us, in our nature, John i, 14. God and man meeting in one person, and being a mediator between God and men. For the design of these words is not so much to relate the name by which Christ should commonly he called, as to describe his nature and office.
Butter — The common food of children in that country. He - The virgin's son. Know - To discern between things good and evil.

Yea — Not only this land shall be preserved until the virgin's son shall be born, but thine enemies land shall be sorely scourged, and these two kings destroyed within a very little time. This child - Shear-Jashub, whom in all probability the prophet pointed at, and who was brought hither by God's special command, ver. 3. for this very use. The land - The lands of Syria and Israel. Forsaken - So far shall Pekah and Rezin be from conquering thy land, that they shall lose their own lands, and their lives too; which they did within two years after this time, being both slain by the king of Assyria.

glossa.text:
*Ask thee a sign.* ((ID.)) That he who did not believe the prophet might be terrified by the authority of the Lord; as if he should say: It seems hard to thee that most powerful kingdoms should be brought to an end in a short time, and that thou shouldst be delivered, and thy people; but ask thee a sign.

*Ask thee a sign.* Moses received a sign from the earth, etc., *as far as* it looks to both the death of the Lord and his ascension.

*I will not ask.* Not humbly, but proudly. For many are read to have asked signs of the Lord and to have received them; but Achaz answered thus, as having authority: *Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.* Or, he feared that in the sign God should be glorified and the idols made cheap.

*Behold a virgin shall conceive.* ((ID.)) In Hebrew *alma;* in Latin also *alma* is called holy, etc., *as far as* that it arose by violence is plain even to fools.

*Emmanuel.* ((ID.)) Some say that Isaias had two sons, etc., *as far as* for the sake of which the Word was made flesh.

*To reprobate the evil.* ((ID.)) As if he should say: Set in the swaddling-bands of infancy he shall have the discernment of good and evil. By these words we perceive that the infancy of the Saviour did not diminish the divine wisdom in him, although it be said: *But the child advanced in age and wisdom,* that the truth of the human body might be proved: for infancy is no prejudice to the divine wisdom.

*He shall be forsaken,* etc. ((ID.)) as if he should say: The land of Syria and of Samaria shall be laid waste from the invocation of his name, and the house of Juda shall be delivered from the two kings.

notes.text: Joseph — The children of Joseph or Israel. The name of Joseph, the most eminent of the patriarchs, is elsewhere put for all the tribes. Cherubim - Which were by the mercy seat above the ark.

Before Ephraim — Here is an allusion to the ancient situation of the tabernacle in the wilderness, where these tribes were placed on the west-side of the tabernacle, in which the ark was, which consequently was before them.

glossa.text: *Thou that rulest,* etc. ((AUG.)) Here Asaph, enlightened, speaks of the coming of Christ, who converts man, and makes firm the vineyard brought out of Egypt: this is the testimony for them that are changed. ((CASS.)) Above he was fearful, who was praying for the sins of the Synagogue: now he presumes, and to those changed for the better he gives a testimony. This psalm is the testimony of the Synagogue concerning the head himself, and his body. ((ID.)) A prayer for the first coming, through which the reparation of the human race is made. ((ID.)) Being finished, he makes an end. O God, O Son. *Thou that rulest,* spiritually, *Israel,* who see thee, *Give ear,* that is, pour the light of goodness upon us, that we may be bright from thee, who of ourselves are dark. *Joseph.* ((ID.)) Thou leadest the faithful people into the folds of God, as sheep to the pastures, of whom: *And other sheep I have that are not of this fold, and them I must bring, that there may be one fold and one shepherd ((Joan. X))*. Each has its own proper word: Israel *is ruled,* Joseph *is led,* that is, the devout people. *Be made manifest.* ((ID.)) He asks that he who was in the secret of majesty may appear before the Jews through the incarnation, as it had been promised, working in them these powers which are signified by these names, Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasse. ((AUG.)) *Be made manifest before.* Known to the angels, be made known to men.

*Before Ephraim.* ((AUG.)) That is, in the nation of the Jews, where these tribes are, namely before fruitfulness, and before the son of the right hand, that we also may be the fulness of knowledge through charity, which is God; and before Manasse, that is, the forgotten one, that thou mayest now come into his mind, according to that saying: *All the ends of the earth shall remember, and shall be converted.* ((ID.)) *Stir up.* He repeats, etc., *as far as* crucified through weakness, rise again through power. ((CASS.)) *Stir up thy power* of miracles, etc., *as far as* whence: *God is faithful, who suffereth you not to be tempted above that which you are able,* etc. ((I Cor. X)).

*Thy face.* ((AUG.)) This face was veiled to Asaph in the time of the weakness of Christ, and then Asaph was sick, not being able to look upon him veiled with a cloud: of which it is said: *God ascended upon a light cloud,* and he shall enter, or shall go into, Egypt, that is, flesh free from sin; but he enlightened it when he rose again and ascended, and so we are saved.

*How long wilt thou be angry?* ((AUG.)) Wrath passes from the servant, that he may not scourge, as is plain, but that he may not condemn: for wrath endures even toward those converted, but as a wrath that corrects. *For he scourgeth every son whom he receiveth ((Isa. IX, Heb. XII))*.

*Thou wilt feed* ((AUG.)) Here he sets forth the sufferings which the saints are to suffer at the time of the coming. As though he said: Although I long for the coming of Christ, yet at that time we are to suffer many things, because *he fed,* etc. *In measure,* etc. ((AUG.)) According to thy strength, that thou mayest be instructed, not crushed; whence: *God is faithful, who suffereth you not to be tempted above,* etc. ((I Cor. X)). Or, according to the measure of faults.
*Thou hast made us a contradiction.* ((CASS.)) While our neighbours, who are of us, are against us. Our enemies mock us, from all of whom, that we may be saved, *O God of hosts,* etc.
*O God of hosts.* ((AUG.)) It is the way of one who desires, to repeat often what he prays for with such prayers.

notes.text:
Concerning the equality of believers, Jews or gentiles, 16-17 To these three parts, whereof The first is treated of, C.i.18-iv. The second, C.v-viii. The third, C.ix.-xi not only the treatise itself, but also the exhortation, answers in the same order. III. The treatise,

1. Concerning justification, which is, (1.) Not by works, for C.i.18 The gentiles, C.ii.1-10 The Jews, and 11-29 Both together are under sin, C.iii.1-20 (2.) But by faith, 21-31 as appears by the example of Abraham, and the testimony of David, C.iv.1-25

2. Concerning salvation, C.v.-viii.

3. Concerning the equal privileges of Jewish and gentile believers, C.ix.-xi. IV. The exhortation, C.xii.1-2

1. Concerning faith and its fruits, love and practical holiness, 3-21 C.xiii.1-10

2. Concerning salvation, 11-14

3. Of the conjunction of Jews and gentiles,. C.xiv.1-xv.13 V. The conclusion, 14-xvi.25 To express the design and contents of this epistle a little more at large: The apostle labours throughout to fix in those to whom he writes a deep sense of the excellency of the gospel, and to engage them to act suitably to it. For this purpose, after a general salutation, chap. i, 1-7, and profession of his affection for them, chap. i, 8-15, he declares he shall not be ashamed openly to maintain the gospel at Rome, seeing it is the powerful instrument of salvation, both to Jews and gentiles, by means of faith, chap. i, 16, 17. And, in order to demonstrate this, he shows,

1. That the world greatly needed such a dispensation, the gentiles being in a most abandoned state, chap. i, 18-32, and the Jews, though condemning others, being themselves no better, chap. ii, 1- 29; as, not withstanding some cavils, which he obviates, chap. iii, 1-8, their own scriptures testify, chap. iii, 9-19. So that all were under a necessity of seeking justification by this method, chap. iii, 20-31.

2. That Abraham and David themselves sought justification by faith, and not by works, chap. iv, 1-25.

3. That all who believe are brought into so happy a state, as turns the greatest afflictions into a matter of joy, chap. v, 1-11.

4. That the evils brought on mankind by Adam are abundantly recompensed to all that believe in Christ, chap. v, 12-21.

5. That, far from dissolving the obligations to practical holiness, the gospel increases them by peculiar obligations, chap. vi, 1-23. In order to convince them of these things the more deeply, and to remove their fondness for the Mosaic law, now they were married to Christ by faith in him, chap. vii, 1-6, he shows how unable the motives of the law were to produce that holiness which believers obtain by a living faith in the gospel, chap. vii, 7-25, viii, 1, 2, and then gives a more particular view of those things which rendered the gospel effectual to this great end, chap. viii, 3-39. That even the gentiles, if they believed, should have a share in these blessings, and that the Jews, if they believed not, should be excluded from them, being a point of great importance, the apostle bestows the ninth, tenth, and eleventh chapters in settling it. He begins the ninth chapter by expressing his tender love and high esteem for the Jewish nation, chap. ix, 1-5, and then shows,

1. That God's rejecting great part of the seed of Abraham, yea, and of Isaac too, was undeniable fact, chap. ix, 6-13.

2. That God had not chosen them to such peculiar privileges for any kind of goodness either in them or their fathers, chap. ix, 14- 24.

3. That his accepting the gentiles, and rejecting many of the Jews, had been foretold both by Hosea and Isaiah, chap. ix, 25-33.

4. That God had offered salvation to Jews and gentiles on the same terms, though the Jews had rejected it, chap. x, 1-21.

5. That though the rejection of Israel for their obstinacy was general, yet it was not total; there being still a remnant among them who did embrace the gospel, chap. xi, 1-10.

6. That the rejection of the rest was not final, but in the end all Israel should be saved, chap. xi, 11-31.

7. That, meantime, even their obstinacy and rejection served to display the unsearchable wisdom and love of God, chap. xi, 32- 36. The rest of the epistle contains practical instructions and exhortations. He particularly urges,

1. An entire consecration of themselves to God, and a care to glorify Him by a faithful improvement of their several talents, chap. vii, 1-11.

2. Devotion, patience, hospitality, mutual sympathy, humility, peace, and meekness, chap. vii, 12-21.

3. Obedience to magistrates, justice in all its branches, love the fulfilling of the law, and universal holiness, chap. viii, 1-14.

4. Mutual candour between those who differed in judgment, touching the observance of the Mosaic law, chap. xiv, 1-23, xv, 1- 17; in enforcing which he is led to mention the extent of his own labours, and his purpose of visiting the Romans; in the mean time recommending himself to their prayers, chap. xv, 18-33. And, after many salutations, chap. xvi, 1-16, and a caution against those who caused divisions, he concludes with a suitable blessing and doxology, chap. xvi, 17-27. ROMANS

But powerfully declared to be the Son of God, according to the Spirit of Holiness — That is, according to his divine nature. By the resurrection from the dead - For this is both the fountain and the object of our faith; and the preaching of the apostles was the consequence of Christ's resurrection.

By whom we have received — I and the other apostles. Grace and apostleship - The favour to be an apostle, and qualifications for it. For obedience to the faith in all nations - That is, that all nations may embrace the faith of Christ. For his name - For his sake; out of regard to him.
Among whom — The nations brought to the obedience of faith. Are ye also - But St. Paul gives them no preeminence above others.

To all that are in Rome — Most of these were heathens by birth, ver. 13, though with Jews mixed among them. They were scattered up and down in that large city, and not yet reduced into the form of a church. Only some had begun to meet in the house of Aquila and Priscilla. Beloved of God - And from his free love, not from any merit of yours, called by his word and his Spirit to believe in him, and now through faith holy as he is holy. Grace - The peculiar favour of God. And peace - All manner of blessings, temporal, spiritual, and eternal. This is both a Christian salutation and an apostolic benediction. From God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ - This is the usual way wherein the apostles speak, "God the Father," "God our Father." Nor do they often, in speaking of him, use the word Lord, as it implies the proper name of God, Jehovah. In the Old Testament, indeed, the holy men generally said, "The Lord our God;" for they were then, as it were, servants; whereas now they are sons: and sons so well know their father, that they need not frequently mention his proper name. It is one and the same peace, and one and the same grace, which is from God and from Jesus Christ. Our trust and prayer fix on God, as he is the Father of Christ; and on Christ, as he presents us to the Father.
A just man -- a strict observer of the law: therefore not thinking it right to keep her.
Jesus — That is, a Saviour. It is the same name with Joshua (who was a type of him) which properly signifies, The Lord, Salvation. His people - Israel. And all the Israel of God.

They shall call his name Emmanuel -- to be called, only means, according to the Hebrews manner of speaking, that the person spoken of shall really and effectually be what he is called, and actually fulfil that title. Thus, Unto us a child is born — and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, the Mighty God, the Prince of Peace -- that is, he shall be all these, though not so much nominally, as really, and in effect. And thus was he called Emmanuel; which was no common name of Christ, but points out his nature and office; as he is God incarnate, and dwells by his Spirit in the hearts of his people. It is observable, the words in Isaiah are, Thou (namely, his mother) shalt call; but here, They - that is, all his people, shall call - shall acknowledge him to be Emmanuel, God with us. Which being interpreted -- this is a clear proof that St. Matthew wrote his Gospel in Greek, and not in Hebrew. Isaiah vii, 14.

He knew her not, till after she had brought forth. It cannot be inferred from hence, that he knew her afterward: no more than it can be inferred from that expression, 2 Sam. vi, 23, Michal had no child till the day of her death, that she had children afterward. Nor do the words that follow, the first-born son, alter the case. For there are abundance of places, wherein the term first born is used, though there were no subsequent children. Luke ii, 7.

glossa.text:
*Now the generation of Christ.* He sets it down without the addition, "Jesu," that thou mayest understand him of whom the prophet says: *Thy God hath anointed thee.* The name Jesus, which belongs to him substantially, he reserves for the angel, so that he who is afterwards to speak of the conception of the Holy Spirit may the more sublimely set forth his proper name from the office of salvation. *So it was.* As has been said, that from Joseph the origin of Mary, who was also of David, might be made clear: and Christ, not of his seed, is shown as God and man, as man through the genealogy, as God through this, that he was of a virgin by the Holy Spirit. So, I say, it was, as has been written above and will presently be said, as afterwards it is made manifest by signs and prodigies, so that the whole book may demonstrate that God and man was born: which must be believed that it may be understood. For here human sense fails, where there is not nature, but power: he who does not believe does not understand that a virgin brought forth, that the word was made flesh.

*When she had been espoused. ((ORIG.))* She was espoused for this reason, that she might signify the Church, which is virgin and spouse: and that through Joseph, etc., *as far as* the espousal was made some days before the constant cohabitation, and in the meantime she was a wife under the guardianship of her husband.

*Before they came together.* Not that they came together afterwards: as if we should say, before he repented, he was overtaken by death. Not that they came together afterwards; but he shows the time next to the nuptials, in which the solemnities of the nuptials are celebrated.

 *She was found with child.* Joseph found that she was with child, but did not know that it was of the Holy Spirit: since afterwards, as one in doubt, he deliberated to put her away; but the apostle adds this, lest in the meantime a suspicion should creep upon the reader. How this was done, and in what order, or in what city the conception of Christ was accomplished, this, being here passed over, is set forth by Luke.

*Just.* By the faith whereby he believed that Christ was to be born of a virgin, and he willed to humble himself before so great a grace.

That he was just, this is a testimony to the chastity of Mary, so that he who preserves the innocent may be called just: but merciful also in that he was unwilling to make it public, just from his knowledge of her chastity, merciful from fear. He knew that she was blameless: but whence or what the matter was he did not know: and therefore he chose a middle way of escape, that he might neither betray the innocent, nor by consenting to a thing unknown make himself guilty before God. It is true virtue when there is neither mercy without justice, nor justice without mercy, which, separated from one another, fall away.

*And would not have her.* Whom he had espoused, to lead into marriage, lest he should seem to conceal what he did not know. Or to expose her to a punishment in which he knew there was no infamy, because he knew that he had received her a virgin and had kept her untouched.

*But while he thought on these things.* Here we are taught that in uncertain matters we must deliberate long, lest we sin by the rashness of levity. *Behold the angel of the Lord.* Because he thinks thus mercifully, he deserves to be consoled, and his own counsel is changed for a better counsel. *Son of David.* Acknowledge what was promised to the house of David, of which thou art, and Mary also, and see it fulfilled in her. *Fear not.* Although it be as great as thou believest, yet fear not on account of guilt, but embrace her with the regard of charity. *Thy wife.* She was a wife not by intercourse, but by affection, not by the joining of bodies, but by the coupling of souls.

Note that she is called wife from the first pledge of the espousal. It is therefore a matter of dispensation if any one is permitted to marry another after the sacrament of betrothal, and if he can never pay the debt.

Rightly is Joseph called husband, and Mary wife, since in him the affection of love is preserved, which is true marriage, and in her without intercourse there is the fruit of the nuptials.

*It is born in her.* To be born of her is to be brought forth into the light. But to be born in her is to be conceived; or according to the presence of the angel which he has from God: to whom the future is as the past, it is called born. *It is of the Holy Spirit.* The Holy Spirit is called God, and the gift of God, and charity; and charity alone made him to be incarnate.

*She shall bring forth.* Lest Joseph should seem not to be necessary to her, he adds: *She shall bring forth.* And so thou shalt be necessary for her care. *And thou shalt call his name Jesus.* He says the same to this man which he had foretold to Mary, that from the utterance he may set before men as well as women that the promised Saviour has already come. *For he.* The name is interpreted.

*Now this,* etc. That she was espoused to a kinsman: that she was found with child: that a virgin brought forth: that he was called Jesus: that he saves. For the Evangelist says this when all things had already been fulfilled.

*That it might be fulfilled.* The prophecy of Isaiah is a sign of the foreknowledge of God, because what it says is certainly foreknown by God: and therefore it ought to be feared by man. But no sign effects what it designates: but only signifies what it shows, so prophecy does not make a necessity of those things which it foretells, but is a sign of the foreknowledge of God.

((HIER.)) There is no necessity of things from the utterance of the prophets, but only the showing forth of truth. Prophecy did not make a necessity of those things which it says, but is a sign of the foreknowledge of God.

One prophecy is from the predestination of God, which must in all ways come to pass, so that it is fulfilled without our choice: as is this of which we here treat. Another is from the foreknowledge of God, with which our choice is mingled. Another there is which is called a threatening, which is made for a sign of divine punishment, that the elect may flee from the face of the bow, and the incautious justly perish; and this not from foreknowledge: because a thing is known far otherwise than it is threatened as to come.

*Behold a virgin.* The prophet Isaiah marvels, and as it were rousing all from sleep, says: *Behold a virgin shall be with child ((Isa. VII))*. To the Holy Spirit that was present which in time was not yet. *Behold a virgin,* etc. The Jews say that this is not a name of integrity, but of age, a girl. But how then is it a sign? He follows the sense of Isaiah, not the words. In place of "she shall conceive" he sets down: *She shall be with child:* and "they shall call" for "thou shalt call," or "he shall be called."

*Emmanuel.* It is proper to Christ, as is Jesus, because he abides always with those whom he saves, by helping them.

For three causes he supports from the Old Testament the things which he sets down in the Gospel: for testification, that he may have testimony from the law and the prophets: for the confirmation of faith, because we believe more easily when we see fulfilled the things which were foretold: for the joining of the New and the Old Testament.

*And Joseph rising up,* etc. ((BEDA.)) Morally. Whosoever is moved by God, let him break off delays, let him rise from sleep: let him do what is commanded. *He did as he had commanded.* Perfect obedience. He did not only what the angel commanded, but also as he commanded. Obedient by the showing of service and by the effect of love, he is rightly said to have done as he commanded him. *The angel of the Lord.* No place is left for lying, where the office of angels is performed. *And he took his wife,* etc. To avoid the infamy of the virgin, to conceal the coming of the Saviour, for the necessary service of the child at his birth.

*Till she brought forth.* Not that afterwards, which is the more certain: since in many ways he knew that he who was born was God.

Not that he knew her afterwards: but *till* is set for *and,* or for *for ever,* as: *Till I make thy enemies the footstool of thy feet ((Psal. CIX))*. It is said that Joseph could not see Mary face to face, whom the Holy Spirit had wholly filled from the conception. And therefore he did not know face to face her whom he had espoused, until the womb was emptied: of which there is no question here. *The firstborn,* etc. Everything is called firstborn which opens the womb, whether another follow or not. Or the firstborn among all the elect by grace. But properly he is called the only-begotten of God the Father, or of Mary.

registers.label: Spare
lines: A child will be born, and they will call him Emmanuel.
Restore us, O God; let your face shine.
He will be named Jesus, for he saves his people.
Come, let us worship the God who draws near.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Hold this name in your mouth like a promise: Emmanuel — God with us — the name given before the child was born.
We have prayed in the long dark, O Shepherd of Israel: turn your face toward us, let it shine, and bring us home.
An angel steadies a frightened man in his sleep: do not be afraid; name the child Jesus, for he will save.
The waiting is almost over; the One whose name means God-with-us is at the door.

lines: A child is coming; his name is God-with-us.
